title: Using a broody bantam to hatch eggs
subtitle: A broody bantam is a better incubator than most machines. She turns, regulates humidity, and tells you when something is wrong.
excerpt: Pekin bantams, Silkies, and bantam Cochins sit tight and stay broody for the full 21 days of incubation with little management beyond fresh water and feed once a day. They also mother the chicks after hatching, removing most of the brooder work. Here is how to set the broody hen on fertile eggs, manage her through incubation, and bring the chicks on after hatch.
sourceNotes: Lewis Wright, The Practical Poultry Keeper (1867), Internet Archive, chapter on natural incubation. Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (1994), chapter on hatching chicks. RSPCA chicken welfare notes. AHDB Poultry, on-farm hatching guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: The hormonal state in which a hen settles on a nest and refuses to leave, with the intention of incubating eggs. A broody hen has raised prolactin levels, plucks feathers from her breast to improve egg contact, and will sit for 21 days without prompting.
The process of placing fertile eggs under a broody hen and allowing her to incubate them. Also called 'putting a hen on eggs'.

projectSchedule.title: Set the hen
projectSchedule.body: Move the broody hen to a quiet nest box with fresh fertile eggs after dark. She sits through the night and usually settles on the new eggs by morning.

projectSchedule.title: First candle check
projectSchedule.body: Candle eggs while the hen is off the nest eating. Remove clear or blood-ring eggs.

projectSchedule.title: Lockdown
projectSchedule.body: Stop disturbing the nest. The hen will take over from here. Expect pipping from day 19.

projectSchedule.title: Hatch day
projectSchedule.body: Most chicks hatch by day 21. Leave unhatched eggs a further 24 hours before removing.

content.text: A broody bantam manages incubation without any intervention beyond daily food and water. She turns the eggs, maintains the right temperature under her breast, and adjusts humidity through her behaviour. After hatch she broods the chicks under her wings for warmth, shows them food, and protects them for 4-6 weeks. The hatch rate under a good broody typically matches or exceeds a well-managed machine.
A hen is reliably broody when she has sat on the same nest for three consecutive nights. One or two nights is sometimes a false start. A
makes a low clucking sound when disturbed, flattens herself on the nest and spreads her wings slightly, and pecks when you try to reach under her.

Move the broody hen after dark to a quiet, separate space away from the main flock. A small crate or dog crate with a nest box inside works well. In the same shed as the other birds but separated is fine.
Prepare the nest with deep straw. Place 4-6 ceramic or wooden dummy eggs in the nest. Transfer the hen onto the dummies after dark and close her in.
Check the following morning. If she is sitting tight, replace the dummy eggs with fertile eggs. This completes
the hen. A Pekin bantam can cover 5-7 bantam eggs or 4-5 standard eggs comfortably.

Offer food and water once a day in a small container placed in front of the nest. Most broodies leave the nest briefly in the morning to eat, drink, and defecate. This brief departure (10-20 minutes) also allows the eggs to cool slightly, which replicates natural conditions.

If a hen has not left the nest after 24 hours, lift her off and place her in front of the food and water. She will return within minutes. Some hens sit so tight they need this encouragement for the first few days.

Leave hatched chicks under the hen for 24 hours before checking. Chicks hatch with enough yolk reserve to sustain them without food or water for a day; moving them or the hen too soon disrupts unhatched eggs still pipping. Once the hatch is complete, move hen and chicks to a small chick pen with a low feeder and drinker accessible to the chicks but not so large the chicks drown in the drinker.

Reintegrating a hen and chicks with the main flock needs care. Other hens often attack chicks. Run hen and chicks separately for 4-6 weeks until the chicks are large enough to escape attention. At that size the mother hen's protection is largely transferred to the flock dynamic.
